hero.title: Link Charts vs Bitly
hero.subtitle: Bitly's free plan changed in 2025. See what each URL shortener gives you today without paying.
hero.verdict: Bitly is the better-known name, but since February 2025 its free plan shows ads before the redirect and creates at most 5 links per month. Link Charts keeps redirects ad-free, creation unlimited, and full analytics free — including a score that separates human clicks from bots.

changes.intro: Free-plan users felt three concrete changes — and they explain why so many people started looking for an alternative:

items.title: Ads on free links
items.desc: Free-plan links now show an ad page (interstitial) before the destination — including old links created before the change.

items.title: 5 links per month
items.desc: The free plan now creates up to 5 links, 2 QR codes, and 3 custom back-halves per month, and analytics is limited to click counts.

items.title: Basic features moved to paid plans
items.desc: Detailed analytics requires the Core plan (US$ 8/month billed annually, 100 links/month, 30–90 days of retention). Custom domains only start at Growth (~US$ 29/month).

changes.note: Source: Bitly's public pricing pages and official blog, checked in July 2026.

table.disclaimer: Bitly data refers to the free plan and public pricing as of July 2026; subject to change.

choose.linkChartsBody: You want detailed analytics for free with no monthly cap, you won't accept an ad between the click and the destination, and you care about traffic quality (knowing whether clicks are real) and a custom subdomain without paying.
choose.rivalBody: You already pay for a Core or Growth plan, rely on the Bitly ecosystem's integrations, and need the most globally recognized brand.

items.q: What's the best free alternative to Bitly?
items.a: Link Charts is a free alternative to Bitly with more complete analytics on the free plan: geography by city, device, browser, traffic source, and a quality score that flags bot traffic — all in real time, with ad-free redirects.

items.q: Is Bitly really free?
items.a: Bitly has a free plan, but today it creates up to 5 links and 2 QR codes per month, shows only click counts, and since February 2025 it displays ads before the redirect — including on old links. Detailed analytics starts on the Core plan (US$ 8/month billed annually).

items.q: Does Bitly put ads on my links?
items.a: On the free plan, yes. Since February 2025, free Bitly links can show an ad page (interstitial) before reaching the destination, and the change also applied to links created before that date. Link Charts redirects never show ads.

items.q: How do I see which city a link's clicks came from?
items.a: In Link Charts, every short link shows click geography (country and city), plus device and browser, in the real-time analytics panel.

items.q: How do I know if my link's clicks are real or from bots?

hero.title: How to tell if your link's clicks are real or bots
hero.subtitle: Not every click is a person. Learn how to spot automated traffic — and how Link Charts does it for you.
hero.verdict: Bots inflate your numbers and hide who actually cares. Link Charts scores every click from 0 to 100 and separates organic traffic from suspicious traffic automatically.

score.intro: Every click starts at 100 points and loses points for each sign of automation. The result falls into one of three tiers:

tiers.label: Organic
tiers.desc: Behavior consistent with a real person.

tiers.label: Suspicious
tiers.desc: Some signs of automation — worth a look.

tiers.label: Likely fraud
tiers.desc: Multiple signs of a bot or automated click.

score.scoreExplain: Known bots (crawlers, spiders, scrapers) get a 0 outright and land in likely fraud.

signals.sectionTitle: The signals that give a bot away
signals.intro: A human click leaves a coherent trail. These are the signals that most often expose automation:

items.title: Datacenter IP
items.desc: Clicks coming from servers and cloud — not residential or mobile networks — are a strong sign of automation.

items.title: Missing browser headers
items.desc: Real browsers report language and platform. Bots often arrive without that information.

items.title: Clicks too fast
items.desc: Several clicks on the same link within seconds point to a script, not a person.

items.title: Device contradictions
items.desc: When what the browser claims doesn't add up — for example, it says mobile, but the signals point to desktop.

items.title: High-frequency sessions
items.desc: Dozens of clicks in the same session fall outside a normal visitor's pattern.

items.title: Programmatic access
items.desc: Arrivals via API or automation instead of a real click from an app or browser.

auto.sectionTitle: How Link Charts does this for you
auto.body: You don't have to investigate anything by hand. For every click, Link Charts evaluates these signals in real time, computes the quality score, and labels the click as organic, suspicious, or likely fraud. In the dashboard, you filter out suspicious traffic in one click and see your real numbers — for free.

items.q: How do I know if my link's clicks are real or from bots?
items.a: Link Charts scores every click from 0 to 100 based on signals like datacenter IPs, missing browser headers, clicks that are too fast, and device contradictions, and labels each one as organic, suspicious, or likely fraud — automatically.

items.q: What is bot traffic on shortened links?
items.a: It's any click that doesn't come from a person: crawlers, scrapers, automatic previews, and scripts. It inflates the click count without representing real interest.

items.q: Why does my link have many clicks but little conversion?
items.a: It's often bot or low-quality traffic inflating the count. Separating organic from suspicious reveals the number that actually matters.

items.q: Does Link Charts detect fake clicks automatically?
items.a: Yes. Detection happens in real time on every click, with no setup, and the result shows up in the free dashboard as a quality score and tier (organic, suspicious, or likely fraud).

items.q: What does a click's quality score mean?
items.a: It's a 0-to-100 rating that sums up how likely the click came from a real person. The more signs of automation, the lower the score.
